name: Eyebrow shaving for cosplay

card.summary: Cosplayers shave or flatten their natural eyebrows so they can paint on the brows of a character, giving a closer match to the character's face.
card.aka: brow blocking, shaving brows for cosplay
card.note: Regrowth time varies; some cosplayers cover brows with glue or wax instead of shaving.

quick.overview:
Some cosplayers remove their eyebrows so they can draw on a different brow shape, colour or position. Characters from anime, games and comics often have brows that are far thinner, higher, differently angled or coloured than human ones, and a bare brow area gives a blank canvas for makeup.

Cosplay is a costume hobby where accuracy to the character is judged, and makeup falls under accuracy at competitions. Wikipedia notes that shaving brows is described as commonplace among cosplayers for a more accurate look.
quick.how: People shave the brows with a razor or trimmer, then cover the area with foundation and draw the character's brows with pencil or paint. Some prefer to block the brows with products instead so they can keep their own, and wigs, coloured contact lenses and body paint are often combined with it.
quick.risks: Shaved brows can grow back unevenly or take time to fill in, and some people find regrowth patchy. Skin irritation from shaving is possible.

lead: Eyebrow shaving for cosplay is the practice of removing natural eyebrows so a character's brows can be drawn or painted on, producing a closer match to the character's face.[1]

Cosplay is a hobby in which people dress as characters from anime, manga, games and film. Wigs, dyes, coloured contact lenses and makeup are standard tools, and competition judges score makeup under an accuracy criterion alongside hair, costume and props.[1]

Wikipedia describes shaving eyebrows as commonplace among cosplayers, though that statement is uncited there. The wider practice of shaving or plucking brows and drawing them elsewhere has a long history, including Japanese hikimayu from the eighth century.[1][2]

chain: Character's brow shape and colour drawn on
Face reads closer to the character
angle.text: Removing the natural brow gives full control over brow shape, height and colour, which can be matched to a character who has unusual or very different brows.

infobox: Hikimayu (Japan, 8th century), thin brows of the 1920s-30s

paras: After the brows are removed, they are covered with foundation or concealer and redrawn with makeup. The approach sits within a broader cosplay toolkit including wigs, hair dye, coloured and enlarged-pupil contact lenses, and body paint.[1]

Removing brows and drawing them in again predates cosplay. In eighth-century Japan, men and women practised hikimayu, shaving or plucking natural brows and painting them higher on the forehead. Some Elizabethan women removed their brows entirely, and heavily plucked thin brows were fashionable in the 1920s and 1930s.[2]

Anyone shaving brows may find regrowth takes time or looks uneven; a general reference notes plucked hair is claimed to stop growing back, a statement marked as unverified there.[2] Many cosplayers use blocking methods to avoid removal.
